write.desc: This topic proves both halves of the fundamental theorem of calculus, each with its exact hypotheses: differentiating an integral with respect to its upper limit, and integrating a derivative. It shows with examples what fails when a hypothesis is dropped, then derives integration by parts, substitution and Taylor's theorem with integral remainder as theorems. These points belong together because each one is either the theorem itself or follows directly from it.

points.name: The integral as a function of its upper limit
points.what: For f integrable on [a,b], define F(x) = integral from a to x of f. Using additivity and the bound |f| <= M, the learner can prove |F(y) - F(x)| <= M|y - x|, so F is Lipschitz and therefore continuous, even when f is not continuous.
outside: additivity of the integral over intervals and the convention for reversed limits
triangle inequality for integrals and the bound of an integral by the supremum times the length of the interval
epsilon-delta definition of continuity

points.name: Fundamental theorem, part 1: differentiating the integral
points.what: The learner can prove that if f is integrable on [a,b] and continuous at c, then F'(c) = f(c), using one-sided derivatives at the endpoints. The proof writes (F(c+h) - F(c))/h - f(c) as (1/h) times the integral from c to c+h of (f(t) - f(c)) dt and bounds it by epsilon.
outside: definition of the derivative as a limit of difference quotients, including one-sided derivatives
epsilon-delta continuity at a point
monotonicity of the integral

points.name: When f jumps: corners in F
points.what: Using the sign function on [-1,1], whose integral function is |x| - 1, the learner can show that a jump in f gives a corner in F, where the one-sided derivatives are the one-sided limits of f. They can also explain why F can still be differentiable at a removable discontinuity of f, but then F'(c) need not equal f(c). Continuity at c is the hypothesis part 1 needs.
outside: one-sided limits of functions

points.name: Every continuous function has an antiderivative
points.what: The learner can deduce from part 1 that every continuous f on [a,b] has an antiderivative, namely F. Because two antiderivatives differ by a constant, any antiderivative G satisfies integral of f from a to b = G(b) - G(a). This is the evaluation formula for continuous integrands.
outside: a function with zero derivative on an interval is constant (corollary of the mean value theorem)
continuous functions on [a,b] are integrable

points.name: Differentiating integrals with variable limits
points.what: The learner can combine part 1 with the chain rule to prove that if f is continuous and u, v are differentiable, then the derivative of the integral from u(x) to v(x) of f is f(v(x))v'(x) - f(u(x))u'(x). They can state the hypotheses that make this valid.
outside: chain rule

points.name: Fundamental theorem, part 2: integrating a derivative
points.what: The learner can prove that if F is differentiable on [a,b] and F' is integrable, then the integral of F' from a to b is F(b) - F(a). F' does not need to be continuous. The proof applies the mean value theorem on each subinterval of any partition P, which gives L(F',P) <= F(b) - F(a) <= U(F',P), and then squeezes between the lower and upper integrals.
outside: mean value theorem
upper and lower Darboux sums and the definition of the integral as their common sup and inf

points.name: Why the hypotheses of part 2 matter
points.what: The learner can show with examples what each hypothesis of part 2 is doing. F(x) = x^2 sin(1/x) has a derivative that is integrable but not continuous, so part 2 applies although part 4 does not. x^2 sin(1/x^2) has an unbounded derivative, which is therefore not Riemann integrable. Volterra's function, mentioned only, has a bounded derivative that is not integrable. A step function has derivative 0 everywhere except at the jump, yet integral 0 is not equal to F(b) - F(a), which shows that differentiability at every point is required.
outside: differentiability of x^2 sin(1/x) and computing its derivative from the definition
integrable functions are bounded by definition

points.name: Integration by parts as a theorem
points.what: The learner can state and prove that if u and v are differentiable on [a,b] with integrable derivatives, then the integral of u v' equals u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) minus the integral of u' v. The proof applies part 2 to uv and uses the product rule and the integrability of products.
outside: product rule for derivatives
integrability of products of integrable functions and linearity of the integral
differentiable functions are continuous, hence integrable

points.name: Integration by substitution (change of variables)
points.what: The learner can state and prove the following. If phi has a continuous derivative on [a,b] and f is continuous on phi([a,b]), then the integral from a to b of f(phi(t)) phi'(t) dt equals the integral from phi(a) to phi(b) of f. The proof takes an antiderivative of f and applies the chain rule. The learner can explain why phi need not be monotone and why the hypotheses are needed.
outside: chain rule
the continuous image of a closed bounded interval is a closed bounded interval (extreme and intermediate value theorems)

points.name: Taylor's theorem with the integral remainder
points.what: The learner can prove the following by induction on n, starting from part 2 and integrating by parts at each step. If f^(n+1) exists and is integrable on the interval between a and x, then f(x) equals its Taylor polynomial of degree n at a plus (1/n!) times the integral from a to x of (x - t)^n f^(n+1)(t) dt.
outside: Taylor polynomial of a function at a point and higher derivatives

points.name: Integral remainder versus Lagrange remainder
points.what: When f^(n+1) is continuous, the learner can derive the Lagrange form f^(n+1)(c)(x - a)^(n+1)/(n+1)! from the integral form, using the weighted mean value theorem for integrals with weight (x - t)^n >= 0. They can compare the two forms: the integral form is exact and needs only integrability, while the Lagrange form is easier for quick bounds. They can use either form to bound the error of a Taylor approximation.
outside: weighted mean value theorem for integrals
Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange remainder
